One primitive, `CheckContext::canonicalScope()`, now owns the key form: the three maps are built with it and their five readers ask with it. `AgentScopeCoverage::unreadCovering()` compares canonically too — a raw compare there turns a CANNOT-VERIFY back into the confident accusation card#5698 removed — while the RECORDED spelling stays raw, because it is rendered verbatim in the `--format=json` document's `unread_agents[].scopes` (DL-249 contract surface, deliberately untouched). `githubScopeConsumers` is NOT in scope: its compare is scope-vs-`webhook_events`-history, not mapping-vs-scope, and its keys are a JSON-contract surface.

**⛔ Decision 4b — canonicalizing that compare WITHOUT this leg would have been strictly worse than the defect it fixes, and the first cut of this change shipped exactly that (caught on review, before merge).** The three maps' compare is now by identity; **`SubscriptionRegistry::subscribedTo` (`:41`) still is not** — it matches `$sub->scopeId === $scopeId` raw against the delivery's scope, and it is deliberately NOT touched here (a hard gate; bound (c) below). So on an install whose agent YAML and `writeback.json` spell one repo two ways, **every GitHub delivery is dispatched to NOBODY** — `subscribedTo()` returns 0 agents, `DispatchService`'s loop body never runs, the event row is written and nothing else happens: no log, no finding, no alert. Before this entry that install at least got an ORPHANED warn (right conclusion, wrong reason). With the compare canonicalized and nothing put in its place it got **SILENCE and exit 0** — a certified-healthy run over an install that dispatches nothing. That is the DL-265 shape (a leg that examined nothing stops reporting `ok`) **re-minted by the fix meant to close a silent-failure class**, and it sits UPSTREAM of the writeback, where `mappingFor()` is never even reached.

⇒ `CheckContext::$githubScopeSpellings` records every spelling each github scope was subscribed with (**unconditionally** — unlike the three gated maps, because the dispatch consequence is classifier-independent), and `WritebackMappingConfigCheck` emits a distinct **SPELLING SPLIT** warn when a mapping key and an agent `scope_id` canonicalize equal but differ in spelling. It names **both** spellings and the mechanism — the dispatcher matches by EXACT spelling, so only a delivery spelled as the SUBSCRIPTION reaches an agent at all. **Strictly more informative than either state it replaces:** more than the old ORPHANED (which said "add an agent" to an operator who has one) and more than the new silence. It is a new `warn` on a config surface — nothing about what the receiver accepts.

**Decision 5 — `bridge:reconcile --repo` matches the way the writeback matches.** It named the same repo through a raw `isset($mappings[$filter])`, so an operator typing the spelling GitHub accepts got "is not a writeback.json mapping" for a repo they had mapped. It now resolves through `configuredRepoFor()` and **re-keys to the configured spelling**, because the per-repo token probe below it needs the raw key (Decision 2). Operator-facing CLI surface only.

**⛔ Proven the way it fails, because a green suite proves nothing here** — the pre-existing fixtures spell the key exactly as the payload does and pass either way. Four legs, each driven against a mutant that should red it: (1) **case-mismatch positive** — key `owner/Repo`, payload `Owner/repo` — reds on `origin/dev`; (2) ⭐ **the live-shape regression** — keys spelled EXACTLY as the live ones (`PupFuzz/agent-webhook-bridge`, `PupFuzz/kanban-board`) against `PupFuzz/…` lookups — passes on `origin/dev` (it is a regression leg) and **reds against the canonicalize-the-lookup-only mutant, which is the outage Decision 1 exists to prevent**; (3) **collision negative** — reds on `origin/dev` (no throw); (4) **unmapped-repo negative** — reds against an over-permissive mutant (`?? first mapping`). Decision 4's leg is end-to-end through the real `CheckCommand` derivation (agent YAML `Owner/Repo` + mapping `owner/repo`) and reds on `origin/dev` with `Output "ORPHANED" was printed`; Decision 5's reds with exit 1 + "is not a writeback.json mapping".

**Alternatives considered.** (a) **Canonicalize the lookup only** — REJECTED: it is the measured three-repo outage (Decision 1). (b) **Store canonical keys and drop the raw spelling** — REJECTED: it breaks per-repo token resolution for every mapped repo and overturns DL-185 (Decision 2). (c) **Keep the raw key and canonicalize at each of the 12 call sites** — REJECTED (canon #5): the parse site and the lookup are the two places that must agree; 12 patched call sites leave the 13th to re-mint it. (d) **A second `strtolower` local to the writeback** — REJECTED: that is the two-answers defect this closes. (e) **Collapse a collision to the last entry, warn at `bridge:check`** — REJECTED: the check runs when an operator runs it; the wrong board gets written on the next delivery. (f) **Give `bridge:check` a leg reporting a mapping key that matches no repo the bridge has SEEN** (the card's step 3) — **NOT BUILT, deliberately.** With the key matched by identity, the class it was proposed for is closed at the source; what remains is a genuine typo or a renamed repo, and answering that needs a new evidence source (`webhook_events` scope history) with two false-positive generators of its own — a newly added mapping has legitimately seen nothing yet, and the DL-199 retention sweep trims the history a quiet repo's only evidence lives in. That is a check with its own denominator question, not a line of code, and it would sit advisory-over-advisory on the ORPHANED leg, which answers the config-side half exactly rather than heuristically. Filed on card#7124.

**STATED BOUNDS.** (a) **Nothing was exercised against a live kanban instance or a real GitHub delivery in this change** — the payload-spelling claim is the operator's measurement of 349 retained deliveries, recorded on card#7124, not something re-derived here. (b) **The canonicalization is the vendored `ExternalReferenceNormalizer`'s and inherits its bounds** — trim + `mb_strtolower` + a 255-char cap; it is a MIRROR of the kanban authority, so a drift there is a drift here. (c) ⛔ **THE CLASS IS NOT CLOSED, AND ITS OPEN MEMBERS ARE NAMED — not just "a future map" (widened on review; the first wording named only hypothetical copies and is the reason the blocker below went unnamed for a round).** Three raw `owner/repo` compares of this exact shape survive this change:
  1. ⛔ **`SubscriptionRegistry::subscribedTo` (`:41`) — `$sub->scopeId === $scopeId`, the DISPATCH path.** This is the one that matters: it decides whether ANY agent receives a delivery, it sits UPSTREAM of `mappingFor()`, and a miss there is total — the event row is written and nothing is dispatched, with no log, no finding and no alert. **Changing it is a hard gate** (it changes which deliveries the system acts on) and is deliberately NOT taken here. **Until it lands, an identity-match at the CHECK layer does not imply a dispatch-layer match** — which is exactly why Decision 4 pairs the widened compare with the SPELLING SPLIT warn instead of letting a divergence fall silent.
  2. **`WebhookController::` (`:59`) — the `401 scope_mismatch` arm.** A security boundary; correctly out of scope to widen, and a member of the class rather than an oversight.
  3. **`EventConsumerReconciler` (`:86`) — `where('scope_id', $scope)`.** Its case-sensitivity is a **collation** property of the column, not a stated one, so it is the member whose behaviour is least legible from the code.
  No guard reds on a fourth copy. The class item stays open on card#7124 with these three named as its current membership. (d) **`configuredRepoFor()` has one consumer today.** It exists because Decision 2 makes the two spellings non-interchangeable; a consumer that needs the raw key and indexes `$mappings` itself would still be right by accident and wrong by design.

**Consequences:** `WritebackConfig` (canonical index + collision/blank fail-closed in the constructor, `mappingFor` canonicalized, new `configuredRepoFor`); `CheckContext::canonicalScope()` + `$githubScopeSpellings` + the four accumulation sites in `CheckCommand`; `WritebackMappingConfigCheck` (canonical reads + the SPELLING SPLIT leg) and `WritebackBoardStateCheck` read with it; `AgentScopeCoverage::unreadCovering`; `KanbanPromoteReleasedHandler` + `KanbanDependabotCardHandler` re-key through `configuredRepoFor()`; `ReconcileCommand`'s `--repo` filter; `docs/writeback.md` (the mapping-key note under § 2, the spelling-split note, and the `--repo` line) and `docs/config-schema.md` (the `writeback.json` row); `docs/CHANGELOG.md`; **DL-030's "scopeId equals the mapping's repo" clause annotated in place** (it is the authority a maintainer re-derives the ORPHANED leg from, and it is now false — DL-292's precedent one entry earlier). **14 tests added** (6 on the config primitive, 3 on the SPELLING SPLIT leg, 1 end-to-end on the check, 1 on the coverage ledger, 1 on the `--repo` filter, 1 on the promote leg's token spelling, 1 on the dependabot `id:` tag spelling). No migration, no new `.env`, no config key added — an existing key's MATCHING changes, and one previously-accepted config shape (two keys naming one repo; a blank key) is now refused at load.

## DL-295 — the DL number is ALLOCATED from the board counter and vetoed against local checkouts; CI refuses a number already in use, and says out loud what it cannot see (card#7157)

- **Date:** 2026-08-21
- **Status:** implemented (card#7157). **⛔ Operator-approved.** Adds a contributor tool (`bin/decision-log.py`) and a new CI gate (`.github/workflows/dl-collision-gate.yml`) — **it changes what CI accepts for a contributor**, and nothing about what the receiver accepts or rejects. No migration, no `.env` change, no token-scope change, no `app/` file touched.

**The defect.** This repo had no DL-minting tool. `next-dl` lives in the toolkit repo and is not vendored here, so the only in-repo way to pick a number was the maximum `DL-` header in `CLAUDE_DECISIONS.md`, plus one. **That method structurally cannot see a mint that has not been pushed.** Two agents cutting branches off the same `dev` tip read the same maximum and write the same number; neither tree contradicts the other until merge, and by then the loser's number is already in a decision entry, a CHANGELOG line, several commit messages and a PR title. The failure is **silent, permanent and cross-cutting**: nothing rejects it, review cannot see it (each PR's log is internally consistent), and once both land the log has two entries claiming one identifier — an identifier cited across repos, in card titles, and by the writeback's own card-correlation grammar. Measured near-miss 2026-08-21: `card-7127-…` and `card-7138-…` both read max 290; the second only avoided minting 291 because the first's in-flight remediation string surfaced in an unrelated test failure during a mutation run. **The correct outcome there was luck, not method.**

**Decision 1 — the number comes from the board's counter, and the tool REFUSES rather than falling back to a scan.** `bin/decision-log.py next` shells out to the toolkit's `next-dl bridge`, which claims atomically from the board's DL sequence **when that endpoint answers** — the only source that can see a number claimed by another allocator moments ago. ⛔ **When it does not answer, `next-dl` falls back to a `max + 1` scan silently, at rc 0 with an empty stderr, and this tool prints that guess as an allocation** — bound (e) below states it verbatim, with the measurements, and the fix is filed upstream as toolkit card#7214. When that allocator is not on PATH the command **exits 3 and prints nothing on stdout**. It was tempting to fall back to the header scan so the tool always answers; that is precisely the method this entry exists to retire, and performing it under a tool's name would launder the same hazard rather than fix it. The board project (`bridge`) is pinned in the tool, because the bridge sequence is per-board and a caller who has to remember the argument can mint out of the kanban-board sequence instead.

**Decision 2 — the tool VETOES the allocated number against every decision log this host can reach, which is the half the counter cannot do.** An entry written on a branch that was never pushed is invisible server-side, so the counter can hand back a number another agent is already writing. The veto enumerates **this clone's worktrees** (`git worktree list`) plus anything matched by `BRIDGE_DL_CHECKOUT_GLOBS` (default `~/agent-webhook-bridge-*`), and refuses with exit 4 naming the file. **The worktree leg is what the incident needed and no existing tool had:** the three branches involved lived in two throwaway worktrees plus the main checkout, and the toolkit's own offline glob (`~/agent-webhook-bridge-*`) matches only the last of those. **The veto was not exercised on a planted case — it refused a LIVE one.** Run on this branch while the card#7157 dispatch was in flight, `next --peek` reported the counter's next number as 294 and then refused it, naming the `~/agent-webhook-bridge-dev` checkout's `CLAUDE_DECISIONS.md`, which already carried an unpushed `DL-294` entry. Without the veto the next agent to allocate would have been handed a number another agent had already written — the card's incident, reproduced without being staged. When git cannot enumerate the worktrees the tool **warns that the veto is narrower than it looks** rather than degrading quietly — a clean result over an unnamed population reports where the searcher stopped, not the state of the world. Separately, when a local log carries a number at or above the one the counter returned, the tool warns that the counter is BEHIND this host: that allocation is still free, but the *next* one will collide. It is a warn, not a refusal, because the predicate for a refusal is "this number is in use" and nothing wider.

**Decision 3 — the CI gate refuses a number already in use, and its stated scope equals its predicate.** `.github/workflows/dl-collision-gate.yml` runs `bin/decision-log.py check` on every PR and makes exactly two assertions: the log at head uses no number twice (which catches a mint colliding with the PR's own base, because the log is append-only), and no number the PR *adds* is already in use at the **live tip** of the target branch (which catches a number `dev` took after the branch was cut — read by fetching, since neither snapshot the gate already holds contains it). **The snapshot it calls the base is the PR's `base.sha` — the base-branch TIP, deliberately NOT the merge base, which is a different commit** — and "present at head, absent at base" means "this PR minted it" only because the head it is paired with is `github.sha`, the merge of the PR head into that same `base.sha`. The pairing is the invariant, it is owned by the workflow's own comment, and a fixture whose head is a real merge commit pins it rather than leaving it incidental (bound (f)). **⛔ STATED BOUND, and it is the one people assume away: it does NOT catch two OPEN PRs that each mint the same new number.** Neither number is on `dev` yet and neither PR's file contains the other's entry, so both are green; the second reds only when it is re-checked *after* the first merges, which is a re-run, not a consequence of the merge — a PR last checked before that merge carries a stale green. Both halves of that bound are pinned by tests rather than left as prose. The gate is also **not a required status check** until an operator adds it to branch protection; until then it reds visibly but does not physically block a merge.

**Decision 4 — one grammar for `DL-` headers, owned by one file.** The allocator's veto and the gate's predicate ask the same question, so they read headers through the same function. A DL entry is an H2 whose text begins `DL-` and digits — deliberately not a search for the token anywhere, because this log embeds kanban-board cross-references ("Mirrors kanban-board DL-196") that a bare grep counts as bridge entries (measured returning 197 when the real maximum was 188). Headers inside a fenced code block are skipped: an entry that shows what a header looks like is documentation, and treating it as a second entry would refuse the very change that documents this file.

**⚑ Operator-facing note — this hazard is CREATED by parallel dispatch, and the cheap mitigation is legitimate.** A single agent working serially cannot hit it; it appeared the first session two agents were dispatched at one repo, and during the card#7157 dispatch itself the operator had to **hand-assign 294/295/296** to three agents to prevent exactly this. **"Do not run two DL-minting agents at once" is a real resolution and is written down here as one** rather than left as an unstated assumption the next parallel dispatch violates. What this entry buys is that the hazard is no longer *silent* when that assumption is broken — which is the part hand-assignment cannot provide, because it depends on the operator remembering.

**Alternatives considered.** (a) **Vendor the toolkit's `next-dl` into `bin/`** — rejected: it is 336 lines plus a shared library, and a second copy of an allocator that already exists is the divergent-duplication defect this repo keeps filing. Delegating to it keeps one implementation and adds only what this repo needs (the pinned project, the local veto, the refusal to fall back). (b) **A CI gate alone** — rejected as sufficient: it is a backstop that fires after a number is already written into four artifacts, and it cannot see a number claimed but unwritten. (c) **The tool alone** — rejected as sufficient: it is bypassed by anyone who types a number by hand, which is the current default. (a)+(b) together is what the card recommended and what shipped. (d) **Mint from the board's `dl` custom field instead of the counter** — rejected, and it is the reason (a) is not enough on its own: that projection returned null on all 264 board-8 cards when it was checked as a cross-source, so a caller treating it as authoritative would read a confident zero. (e) **Assert that a minted number EXCEEDS the target branch's maximum** — rejected: the operator hand-assigns blocks, so the PR carrying 295 legitimately lands after the one carrying 296. The predicate is "already in use", never "must be highest", and a test pins that a lower-but-free number passes.

**STATED BOUNDS.** (a) The gate reads three files and knows nothing about a number **claimed from the counter but not yet written** into any log, and nothing about a checkout on **another host**; `next` covers the first and neither covers the second. (b) The veto's population is this clone's worktrees plus one glob — a checkout outside both is not covered, and the tool says so when it cannot enumerate them. (c) `next` was exercised against a **fake allocator** on PATH: what is tested is what this tool does with the number it is handed, not the toolkit's claim path or the board endpoint behind it. (d) Appending entries at end-of-file means two agents minting concurrently will hit a **git merge conflict** in this file. That is deliberate and is the good failure — visible, at merge, before either number is final.

(e) ⛔ **THE ATOMICITY IS THE ALLOCATOR'S AND IT IS CONDITIONAL — and its condition fails SILENTLY, which is the one silent failure mode left in a change whose whole thesis is that the retired method failed silently.** The bound is `next-dl`'s own, recorded verbatim rather than paraphrased. Its header: *"If the endpoint is absent (older kanban / not deployed) or unreachable, it falls back SILENTLY to the offline max+1 scan"*, and *"the offline path is NOT atomic — safe for single-stream allocation; concurrent allocators on a shared board need the claim endpoint (the default) to avoid duplicates"*. Its transport says the same at the two arms that take that path: `resp="$(curl …)" || exit 1` — *"connection failure → benign fallback"* — and `kb_is_uint "$val" && [[ "$val" -ge 1 ]] || exit 1` — *"2xx but no positive value → benign fallback"*. Only a non-2xx other than 404 aborts. On the benign arm `next-dl bridge` prints a `max + 1` guess, **exits 0, and writes nothing to stderr**, and `bin/decision-log.py next` prints it as an allocation: two agents there get one number, which is this card's own defect wearing a tool's name. **Both halves measured, 2026-08-21, not inferred.** The live board answers `GET /boards/8/dl-sequence.json` with HTTP 200 `{"board_id":8,"last_value":289,"live_max":296,"next":297}`, so the endpoint IS deployed and today's primary path is genuinely atomic — the silent path needs a 404 or a connection failure on the CLAIM route. Against a stub board answering 404 there, `next-dl bridge` printed `DL-0294` at rc 0 with an empty stderr and `decision-log.py next` printed `DL-294`. **Recorded here, deliberately not cross-checked in this repo**, and the alternative was measured rather than argued: under the same stub `next-dl bridge --peek` printed `DL-0294` too, because both routes degrade to the SAME offline scan — a claim-vs-peek compare would therefore agree exactly when the hazard is present, which is a decoration, not a check. Reading the endpoint directly from here would mean re-implementing the toolkit's board-config resolution and auth — alternative (a), already rejected above. The distinction exists only inside `next-dl`, which knows which arm answered, so the fix is filed where it can be made: **toolkit card#7214** (`--require-counter` strict mode plus a loud fallback). Until that ships, this is the bound, and `cmd_next`'s docstring and its refusal text carry it where an author meets the tool.

(f) **The gate's base is the PR's `base.sha`, and its correctness rests on a pairing GitHub supplies, which nothing in this repo can verify.** Head is the working tree at `github.sha` — the merge of the PR head into that same `base.sha` — and only that makes `added` the PR's mints. Should the two ever disagree, a `base.sha` OLDER than the merge commit's base parent makes entries the base branch already carried read as this PR's mints (a loud, visible false refusal), and a NEWER one drops entries from `added` (a silent missed catch). `DlCollisionGateTest` pins the invariant on the inputs the step is handed — a fixture whose head is a real merge commit, with the fork point as the control that reds — but it cannot pin what GitHub hands it. Measured on this repo, 2026-08-21: `base.sha` is genuinely not the merge base — PR #542's `fe562910` is not even an ancestor of its head branch `270c236f`, whose merge base is `61e40d85` — which is why nothing in this change calls it one. Rewriting the step to derive its base with `git merge-base "$BASE" HEAD` is inert while the pairing holds (`$BASE` is then an ancestor of the merge, so `merge-base` returns `$BASE`; measured — every case stays green), and that is exactly what makes it dangerous: the first caller whose head is not that merge gets the fork point and the false refusal. The workflow comment says so at the line.

**Consequences:** new `bin/decision-log.py` (`next` + `check`, stdlib-only) and `bin/test_decision_log.py` (29 cases, wired into `bin/ python unit tests` by discovery — no enumeration to update); new `.github/workflows/dl-collision-gate.yml` with **no `paths:` filter**, deliberately, since a filter that stopped covering this log would make the gate absent rather than red (DL-283's measured failure mode); new `tests/Feature/Workflows/DlCollisionGateTest.php` (10 cases) executing the real workflow bash against a throwaway origin + clone, so the fetch of the live target tip is genuinely exercised and the CI pairing is built from a real merge commit rather than approximated; this file's header gains the minting method; `CLAUDE.md` standing rule 2 and the quick-start block point at it.
